utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth and the interpreters; good morning to the Registry staff, the counsel for the Defence and the Prosecution; good morning, General Krstic. We are here to take up our proceedings. We are in open session, and we're going to have the witness shown in. The witness is from yesterday. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, good morning; good morning, Your Honours; and good morning, Counsel. This witness was testifying yesterday in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Let us move into private session then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to take advantage of this opportunity, without entering into the debate, that we ought to be mindful of the fact that this is an international trial, and very frequently national systems are not applicable here, simply speaking. And according to the Statute, national laws are not applicable here. They can be used to interpret our Statute. But having said that, let me give the floor to Mr. Visnjic, because I think that there has been something new presented by Mr. Harmon. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to refer to what Mr. Harmon said a moment ago, but I would try to do that by linking it up to the concrete situation we find ourselves in. Perhaps the Prosecution finds themselves in a difficult position when the Prosecution did not have this previous statement of the witness. But General Krstic did give his statement, in which he speaks about these circumstances and presents his views and positions, and I think at one point, when asked by Mr. Ruez, when asked whether he would repeat that under oath, he said he would. So General Krstic gave that statement before the beginning of this trial, before the trial went ahead. So the Prosecution cannot put itself in -- cannot say that it was surprised by developments and that it was not able to foresee that the Court would need all the evidence relating to the facts and the circumstances. And in that sense, the Defence does not consider that the Prosecution was duty-bound to envisage in advance every evidence that could appear in the case in-chief. Quite the contrary, the Defence considers that this particular piece of evidence was highly foreseeable, bearing in mind that General Krstic, before the start of trial, in actual fact, presented his position with regard to these facts and circumstances. He stated his views. And this also refers to some of the other facts that are the subject of evidence in the Prosecution's rebuttal, but I would just like to adhere to this particular fact and circumstance for the moment. Therefore, the tension that was mentioned by the Prosecutor as existing and linking that tension up to their efforts to present their evidence, I think in this particular case do not hold water because General Krstic has, in fact, laid open his position before the case in-chief went ahead. So the Prosecutor had sufficient time and should have had sufficient evidence at that time, might I say, although I don't want to enter into that realm, but he was able to foresee the further running of the proceedings, bearing in mind General Krstic's initial statement. So I do not feel that the Prosecution was taken by surprise in any way by the position taken by General Krstic or the position of the Defence either, in view of the cross-examination which, in fact, went to overrule the facts that the Prosecution put forward. What I wish to say, on the other hand, is that the indictment -- that is to say that the Defence is faced with tension now because suddenly we have a certain quantity of evidence and exhibits which should have been used in the case in-chief, and now that enormous quantity of material and evidence is placing us in -- is taking us back to something that we thought we had gone through a long time ago. So they're taking us back to the case in-chief. And this kind of conduct and behaviour is precisely the kind that will make it difficult for us to arrive at the end of the trial, because the Prosecution can continue unearthing new evidence, and the positions were clear from the beginning with respect to the Defence and the Prosecution. I can only envisage the Prosecution's disquiet in one case, that is to say, had the Defence not stated its positions but kept silent and waited for the Prosecution to present its evidence, but we had quite the reverse situation, because from the very beginning, our client made statements as to facts and circumstances. So the Prosecution was left in no doubt as to what will happen in the case in-chief. And quite the reverse; the Defence considers that the Prosecution did present evidence precisely on the basis of what General Krstic had said and that in that sense, it narrowed down the quantity of evidence and not expanded it. And let me remind the Trial Chamber of the evidence put forward with respect to the grave sites and certain facts and circumstances which it was quite evident that on the basis of General Krstic's statement we did not contest. We never contested that certain things took place. It was just the circumstances, perhaps, but some facts were never contested from the very beginning by us. On the other hand, with respect to the facts and circumstances regarding the conversation, whether the General became Commander on the 14th or 13th, I think that he stated this quite clearly in what he said and in fact opened his evidence on that part so that the Defence had a very clear-cut situation because we had the statement from the General himself. Thank you. I have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, we should bring this to a close, this debate to a close. We did not envisage having a debate on this issue at this point, but as we have opened the debate already, I'm going to give the floor for the last time to Mr. Harmon to wind up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would just like to correct the record. We did take a statement from General Krstic - it has been admitted as an exhibit - and an examination of that statement will reveal no description of any ceremony that took place on the 13th of July or the 14th of July. The first time a ceremony was raised in this trial was during the cross-examination -- during the direct examination of the accused, when he described a ceremony where General Mladic appointed him Commander, and then he limited it, of the Zepa operation. So the first time that was raised was in the direct examination of the accused. The evidence that is being put in goes to two issues, one, the general timing; but, two, it directly contradicts what General Krstic testified under oath about a ceremony that took place at Vlasenica on the 13th of July. So I want the record to be perfectly clear as to when the issue of the ceremony itself was presented. It was presented in the Defence case for the first time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now one final word, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one sentence, continuing on from Mr. Harmon. The Defence wishes to stress another fact, and we'll leave it to the Trial Chamber to judge, but General Krstic, in his statement, directly stated that he became Commander at a ceremony which occurred on the 20th or the 21st in the restaurant called Jela. So the Defence considers that that was sufficient basis for the Prosecution to contest that fact in its case in-chief. Yes. That was in the statement given to Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, on the 18th and 19th of February, 2000, which means before trial, for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Thank you. We're not going to rule on the admission of this evidence which has been tendered by Mr. Harmon at this point. As you know, the Chamber will address the issue of several pieces of evidence in order to rule on this matter. Do we have another witness, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey will take the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. The next witness is a Captain Koster. He is a Dutch officer that testified at the Rule 61 hearing, and we played his video, and just as our background road map, he will be called on to rebut the testimony of Witness DB, who [redacted] who testified that he drove through Potocari on the evening of 11 July with his COMS van and saw a large crowd of people around the compound and saw VRS soldiers mixed within it, and this witness will be called just very briefly, in a few brief questions, to rebut that. And the principal parts of Witness DB's testimony we intend to rebut are on transcripts page 7256, 7080 through 7085, and 7255 through 7259, and 7319, and with that, I think we are ready to call this witness. If we could have the exhibit, the aerial exhibit, that we had set aside for him. I hope we've got the ELMO up and going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, would you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You should have an exhibit, an aerial exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Captain Koster. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please read the solemn declaration that the usher is giving you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Captain, for having come here. You will first be answering questions that will be put to you by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, your witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Captain Koster, what is your current position?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: My current position is being a company commander of a 13th Air Mobile Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you in the Dutch army back in July of 1995, stationed in the Potocari compound in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the Court is familiar with your initial testimony that you gave some time ago, so we won't go into a whole lot of background on that, but can you tell us on July 11th what your particular assignment was in the afternoon, evening hours?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I can. My assignment was actually being the commander of the troops who were outside the compound and guarding and guiding the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many troops did you have under your command?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Approximately 50, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we're putting Exhibit 769 on the ELMO. I don't know if this is going to the outside, but I notice the witness's face is distorted, which is not necessary. As I'm searching to find the ELMO, I notice that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness will testify in public, so appropriate measures need to be taken in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It is not distorted. You just pushed the distort button. That's why. The technician just informed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the issue has been resolved now. However, there seems to be a little problem. When we are watching the video, we see that we are in public session, but when we press the button for the ELMO, we see a distorted image on the ELMO. We should like to see the video and not the distorted image of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first button.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The first button, I have a nice shot of Judge Rodrigues. The second one I have a distorted shot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar -- yes, that's what we can see, on the second button, the video, but we would like to have the ELMO, the overhead projector, which is the second button, and on the second button there seems to be nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I know when we switch courtrooms these things happen. I requested prior to trial that these be looked into, and I hope we could finish. We can certainly go through testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have it now. Yes, but we have lost a lot of time. Mr. McCloskey made sure that the equipment is checked, but we still wasted a certain amount of time. But without much further ado, let us proceed now. Mr. McCloskey, I think that we are ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Captain Koster, if you could just take a look at this exhibit, and there's a pointer there. Do you recognise this scene?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could you, with your pointer, point out the area where you were stationed and your troops were responsible for the afternoon or evening hours of July 12th, 1995.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. For me myself, I was positioned in this particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Near the crowd that's marked "people"?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir. Also we had troops over here. We had troops --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You need to sort of indicate, if you could, so we can tell from the record where you're talking about, just by something on the photo.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Okay. Troops guarding the people, troops in the vicinity of the holes of the former bus station, and also troops here, at the end of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That would be about how many metres down from where the crowd of people is in this shot?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: From this position to there, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. From the people down there.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I guess it's about a hundred -- two hundred metres, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what hours were you on duty in that area on the afternoon/evening of July 11th?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Eleventh. From the 11th, the afternoon, sir, I was on duty until approximately 8.00 p.m., and then I went up to the compound for approximately two hours, and then returned to my position, where I stayed the whole night, the morning, the afternoon of the 12th of July, and also the evening of the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps I made a mistake and I asked him about the 12th the first time. I meant the 11th, which he has responded to. Thank you, Captain Koster.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, while you were gone from the area briefly on the evening of the 11th, did you have a deputy that was in command while you were gone?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, on the afternoon or evening hours of July 11th, was there any vehicular traffic from the VRS military along that road?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No, sir. I have not seen any vehicle movement, VRS vehicle movement on that road, and neither I was reported to by my deputy on the 11th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there some sort of roadblock or checkpoint there?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. We installed sort of a roadblock to guide and to guard the refugees, so a vehicle couldn't get through without being reported to me, without being seen by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would this have been a significant event if a VRS vehicle had come through this area on July 11th?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you notice any VRS soldiers in this area around where the people are, or anywhere around this compound, around this road, on the afternoon or evening of July 11th?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Not on July 11th, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Would that have been a significant event if VRS soldiers had been amongst those people or in this area?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I would have seen them, I would have been reported, and also I guess the refugees would have panicked. So it's not been reported and I have not seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you be sure that no VRS vehicle came through this area and no VRS soldiers were in this area on the evening or afternoon of July 11th?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure about it, on the 11th; yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about on the 12th? What was the scene on the evening hours of the 12th, perhaps between 6.00 p.m. and 10.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: In the evening we were told by the VRS that we had to clear the road from the refugees. The refugees had to stay off the road. So we did. We kept the people off the road. And that's about it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So did you lose control of the road on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, we did, sir. It was in the afternoon when the VRS started to transport the refugees. Then we lost control of the road, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time in the afternoon did you lose control of the road?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, the VRS arrived approximately 1.00 in the afternoon, and I guess it would be one hour, one and a half later, then we lost control of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So in the evening hours of July 12th, could there have been VRS traffic along that road in this area on the diagram by the "people"?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were there VRS soldiers in this area on the evening hours of July 12th, around where the "people" are marked?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were. In the early evening and later on there were VRS soldiers. I've seen some trucks and some jeeps passing by and -- that's about it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. For the Defence, Mr. Petrusic. Captain Koster, you will now be answering questions put to you by Mr. Petrusic, who is representing the Defence in this case. You have the floor, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Captain, in the evening of the 19th -- that is, the 11th of July - I apologise - between 1900 and 2100 hours, were you personally present on the road which we can see here on this aerial photograph, that is, the road through Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I went to the compound at approximately 2000 hours, so until that time, I was patrolling in that area near and on the road, yes, sir, until 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was there any barricade, any obstacle set up on this road which prevented the vehicles from passing through?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. We made a sort of a roadblock, just by military persons, to provide the refugees going up to Bratunac. That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have received the correct interpretation. You said that you had set up a kind of roadblock in order to enable refugees to go to Bratunac; is that what you said, Captain?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Captain, this Chamber has heard Witness DB, who, on page 7078 of the transcript, stated as follows, that is, that the forward command post at Pribicevac was abandoned by him around 1900, or sometime later. And further on, on page 7081, in response to a question put to him by the Defence counsel whether he had passed through Potocari, he stated, "Yes." In response to a further question as to what had happened to the members of UNPROFOR, whether they prevented anyone from passing through Potocari, he stated, "I did not encounter any control, or anything similar, in Potocari itself." And then in the next question, as to whether he personally had seen civilians in the town of Potocari, he stated, "Yes. In the town of Potocari, both on the left and the right side of the road, I saw a huge number of civilians." Now, you are telling us that not a single vehicle, not a single soldier of the VRS, had passed through the area in that period of time. Is it your testimony that this witness, whose statement I have just read to you, his testimony that was given before this Chamber, are you saying that this witness was not telling the truth?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object to that question. It is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It can be restated and have the same meaning, clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Petrusic, would you please rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Captain, in relation to your statement, to your testimony, is it possible that a vehicle of the VRS carrying several soldiers could have passed through Potocari on the 11th of July after 1900 hours?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No, sir, because they had to move up through the crowd, and they had to pass the so-called roadblock, and I would have known. I informed my former colleague to make sure what I am telling, and it has never been reported to me that a vehicle moved up on the 11th of July, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So you didn't receive any report on the movement of that particular vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No, sir, not when I was there and not when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this concludes my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Any additional questions, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Judge Fouad Riad? Madam Judge Wald? Captain Koster, we don't have any further questions for you. Thank you very much once again for having come here. We wish you a lot of success in your work. It seems that our usher has left the room. Here, he's back. Mr. Usher will now show you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, what happens next?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, by the silence of Defence counsel, I see we do not have any objection as to the rebuttal evidence here, so I take it there is no objection as to the rebuttal -- this coming in as appropriate rebuttal evidence. And if there is, I would obviously like a chance to argue it; and if there is not, I can go on to the next issue. I only note that because we've been getting oral challenges to these things without notice before, and I just want to be very clear that this is at rest at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. McCloskey. Please abstain from commentary; that is more appropriate. The question is, this exhibit, 769, Exhibit 769, was it a new one or has it already been tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is an old exhibit that's already in, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. So you don't wish to have it admitted, that is to say, there's no -- and there's no reason to go into comments of the kind you made. I don't know whether the Defence would like to say anything at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with respect to the witness who has just completed his testimony, may I say that according to the opinion of the Defence, this is a classical example of a rebuttal witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us end the debate there, and we shall reserve allegations for the end of the proceedings. Mr. McCloskey, who do you have for us next?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have Mr. Butler, who we're all familiar with, but before we get to Mr. Butler, I had a clarification of a couple of exhibits that we put off the other day, and I hope I can make some sense out of this. It has to do with the three conversations of August 2nd regarding -- General Krstic and Popovic were two of the conversations, and then there was a third conversation between General Krstic and someone named Mandzuka, and that Mandzuka intercept was Exhibit 862A. And as I'd given the Court an outline at the various times we received this material, I just have one clarification. The Mandzuka exhibit, 862A, was a conversation that was in the notebook, Exhibit 748, which was a notebook that had the so-called "Kill them all," and that was a notebook that we had for quite awhile. This particular conversation was not called to our attention until Mr. Harmon found it earlier this week, and it's unclear when it was actually dated and in the database. But just to clarify that last conversation, because it is, I believe, the subject of the Defence motion. So that's the end of that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what action comes next?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can give a brief road map of Mr. Butler's testimony and some of the points that he'll rebut, prior to his arrival. There are some six or seven points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps, Mr. McCloskey, we could hear the witness at this point. Shall we hear the witness, and the witness can explain all that us to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He basically understands what the legal team is asking him to rebut, so I think he can -- he will do that. However, he's not going to be able to give you our legal view of that, but he knows the areas that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall we have the witness brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's one other small issue that I've discussed with the Defence. Mr. Butler will be testifying about some small pieces of hearsay evidence that will clarify some of his prior testimony and that go to some issues that I've spoken to the Defence about, that they didn't have any objection to, and it will actually help make the procedures go smoother and actually -- so they don't have to bring in witnesses on surrebuttal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we hear the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has understood Mr. Butler's testimony in two parts. One part would be the refuting of certain facts which the Defence put forward in its case, and the second part, let us call it exculpatory material that the Prosecution arrived at at later stage and which it wishes to present in one way. Of course, it will be up to the Trial Chamber to assess this, whether that is in order. But Mr. McCloskey said that Mr. Butler will be speaking about seven topics, and in the summary of his statement, I have four topics. Now, that four plus three additional topics, or is it seven subjects, seven topics in the rebuttal part of the Prosecution? And I'd like to ask Mr. McCloskey to tell us briefly about what Mr. Butler is going to contest in his testimony. What he's going to rebut, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, my numbering system included these issues of what counsel has referred to as exculpatory. We would, of course, disagree with that, and it was not my intention to be putting this material up as exculpatory, but it was my intention to save time and effort on all parties. If counsel chooses us not to do this, they may call these witnesses that we've alerted them to, and I'm satisfied with leaving it at that. If he would like to go with our original agreement, I would go with that too. I thought we had an agreement, and I may have been mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my comment did not refer to this addition that Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Harmon, myself, and my colleague agreed upon. My understanding was with respect to what was given in the summary of what Mr. Butler will be testifying to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Those are the points on which the witness is going to testify. I think we are not hearing each other. It is a conversation between two deaf sides. So are we talking about the points that the witness is going to talk about, testify to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There you have it, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think Mr. Visnjic and I agree with each other and have an agreement, so I'll just take that as it goes and explain what the rebuttal points will be. The first point would go to rebuttal testimony related to the testimony of Professor Radinovic on transcript 7880 through 7882, relating to directives 70 and 71. And if you recall, those are the directives - one's signed, I believe, by Karadzic and the other by Mladic - the first one regarding the Drina Corps directive to make life unbearable for the people in the enclave. Professor Radinovic talked about those two and their relationship with each other. Mr. Butler would like to rebut some of the testimony that Radinovic had regarding that. That's number one. Number two also has to do with Professor Radinovic who testified on 782 -- excuse me, transcript 7832 through 7833, and 8107 through 8114, and this is a brief subject where he discussed that the objectives of the VRS in 1992 and 1993 were purely defensive, and he also stated at some point in the testimony, and I don't have the exact transcript, that refugees move with war and that that was not a result of any particular policy or practice by the VRS. We have recently identified another directive from the VRS signed by General Mladic that will rebut these particular contentions of Professor Radinovic. This was something that -- it's a directive number 4 from -- I believe it's November of 1992, that was obtained among thousands of documents a few years ago and was just recently translated into English. So we were allowed to identify it, and we noticed that -- we believe that it clearly rebutted what Professor Radinovic was referring to. Then I was going to ask Mr. Butler to give his interpretation of the intercept mentioned by the Defence just recently between Zivanovic and Bogicevic to clarify his view of that. And then we have an issue directly rebutting the testimony of General Krstic, where, in response to questions by Judge Wald, he stated he was not aware of any prisoners being taken on 12 July by the VRS. And we have identified two documents from the Zvornik Brigade that shed light on that issue, one intelligence document dated 12 July that is a report to the Drina Corps Command that talks about this issue. These were documents that Mr. Butler missed in his analysis and were identified somewhat recently as being direct rebuttal to this very important point. And then, lastly, it was my intention, if the Court deems appropriate, to ask Mr. Butler about his analysis of the "Kill them all" conversation, if this issue is still of concern to the Court and if they would like to hear from Mr. Butler, as they did from Ms. Frease on that point. If that issue is put to bed, I don't need to ask him, but if counsel intends to and the Court is interested, I can certainly ask him about those issues also. And that's it. And oh, just -- we have the representative from the United States [Realtime transcript read in error "United Nations"] that would also, as before, would like to sit in with the testimony of Mr. Butler. We have talked about that, and the Defence has no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It said in the interpretation "the representative of the United Nations," but I think it was "United States," was it not? So I think we all agree on that point. Yes. Mr. Visnjic, I think you've heard practically the whole testimony of Mr. Butler. Now, do you know the points that Mr. Butler is going to testify to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we're going to have to dwell on this question, because none of those points, conditionally speaking -- that is to say, most of the points stated by Mr. McCloskey do not exist in the summary that the Defence has received from the Prosecution as to Mr. Butler's testimony, and it is dated the 8th of January, I think, the document dated the 8th of January. Now I am going to say what Mr. Butler is expected to testify according to what we have received. Mr. Butler will testify to the fact that Vinko Pandurevic was appointed Commander of the Tactical Group deployed for the Srebrenica operation - that's one point - and that he will talk about tactical groups generally. The second point, it says Mr. Butler will present the other orders identifying the operative groups and tactical groups and will explain their importance. The third point, according to this document, Mr. Butler will identify the tank in Sandic Polje. Point 4, Mr. Butler will explain two intercepts of the 2nd of August between General Krstic and Colonel Popovic. According to what Mr. McCloskey has just told us, Mr. Butler will be talking about directives 7.0 and 7.1, which is a subject that we are absolutely not prepared for. According to what Mr. McCloskey has told us, Mr. Butler will also speak about the goals and targets of the Army of Republika Srpska. That is a topic that I'm hearing for the first time now. Another thing Mr. McCloskey said: Mr. Butler will be interpreting radio messages, Zivanovic/Bogicevic, and I can only conditionally say that it could be the subject of some kind of rebuttal, although that message was stressed by the Defence and with respect to time, the time when it was recorded, and not with respect to its contents. Again, Mr. Butler will -- it seems that he will be speaking about some prisoners of the 12th of July. That is something I'm hearing for the first time once again here, and an analysis of the "Kill them all" statement would be another question that would be raised by the Prosecution or Defence. So at this point in time we're hearing for the first time that Mr. Butler is actually going to testify about three or four of the five points that Mr. McCloskey mentioned, and not four or all four points that were indicated to us in the summary of his statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, let us go to the testimony. What is the testimony about? Is what Mr. Visnjic has just said true? Is that correct? I have read your summary and I have identified the points that Mr. Visnjic has just enunciated. I don't have your witness list and the summaries here, but I remember that. Would you like to reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is to say, why you have modified the contents of the testimony or the summary of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will apologise. Mr. Visnjic is largely correct. The material -- the summary that reflects most of this stuff must not have been transferred to the Defence, and I apologise. I meant it to be. I've discussed these matters with counsel -- some of the matters with counsel. For example, the operative directive by Mladic, we've provided that to them well in advance and we've discussed it, and so they were fully aware that that was an issue. I've also -- we've also provided them the two July 12th documents that I've referred to and as part of the rebuttal evidence, and the parts about 7, 7.1 were in my initial summary, which I have apparently failed to provide to the Defence, and I apologise, so they do not have any notice of that. And the intercept between Bogicevic and Zivanovic was just as a result of the most recent Court material. So I do apologise. They have not had the part about 7 and 7.1, and we can disregard that. It's not a major point. They have had the part about operative directive of General Mladic. We have discussed that with them. They should have been prepared for it, though I do fully acknowledge they were not given a written -- which was our practice when these things happened, to give them a supplemental, and we did not do this. I'm sorry. These last few days have been hectic, and that is my fault. So that leaves us with the two critical parts of Mr. Butler's rebuttal testimony, the July 12th documents and the operational directive, which the Defence has had as part of our rebuttal case, were given specifically as part of our rebuttal case. I've discussed the operative directive briefly with them, but he's absolutely correct; I did not apparently submit the supplemental witness statements, which I should have, and I apologise for the Court for this grievous error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At all events, Mr. McCloskey, you are fully aware of the fact that the rebuttal ends today, regardless of what can turn up. Now, the Chamber announced a long time ago that your rebuttal will be closed today, so I stand by that. You have raised this issue, something that was not foreseen. It was not foreseen. There was no reason to modify. So let me ask the Defence: Do you accept the apologies of Mr. McCloskey and would you give him the opportunity of having his rebuttal on the questions he has announced, or do you maintain your position as to the initial motion, your initial motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me say that I have absolutely been taken by surprise and I am not prepared to tackle any topics that are not the subject of this summary. I say this with all honesty and frankness. Mr. McCloskey said he might have talked to us about the directive issued by Mr. Mladic. Perhaps that was two months ago, when some material was given to us - I don't remember - because we keep getting documents and material from the Prosecution, so I don't know when we got this directive. But just like the Prosecution does, I placed it on a shelf, and I knew that this would not be the subject of a debate of any kind. It is a document of several hundred pages. I didn't want to waste my time on that massive pages, because it wasn't listed on the topics to be discussed today. Now, how can I be prepared for something that was not written down? And I think that is totally out of order, in view of the time that we have and the speed that we need, the schedule that we have placed before us. So we are absolutely unprepared to proceed except on the topics that were included in the summary given to us by the Prosecution, so that I cannot accept this, not because I wouldn't want to and don't want to, but because I am not prepared to do so. Yesterday and the day before, the Prosecution failed to inform us of these topics then either. I just happened to ask by chance Mr. McCloskey as to the other part, the Sandic tank, the tank at Sandici [as interpreted]. I wanted to clear that up and I wanted to clear up whether some of these questions and topics have been dealt with in the case in-chief, which we do with every witness of late. As to this, I am completely taken aback, and it is totally unacceptable for me to proceed. Mr. President, I have just been informed that General Krstic has asked for a break. If we might take a break for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just one question, Mr. Visnjic. Leaving out the first two topics which dealt with the Radinovic testimony and the accompanying new Mladic directive, I'm not sure I understand why, if Butler is simply going to give us his interpretation of the Zivanovic/Bogicevic intercept, which you yourself brought to our attention, and he's just going to give us his analysis of the August 2nd "Kill them all," which we've all talked about ad infinitum, I'm not quite sure why you need too much time to prepare for that. And I have more question about, but some doubt about, whether or not, if the specific rebuttal evidence to the question of prisoners being taken and General Krstic's knowledge on the 12th, if you've had those documents. I mean, is it true you feel that you can't even cross-examine Butler on his interpretation of these intercepts, which we've talked about continually over the last five days? I understand your Radinovic arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Wald, to respond to your question: On the interpretation of the radio messages Zivanovic/Bogicevic, and an analysis of the "Kill them all" statement, I -- that is to say, I just was conditionally opposed to the first conversation. As to the second, I said that perhaps the Defence could take advantage of this opportunity to ask Butler some questions about that. So that particular conversation -- it is not that we are not -- that we are absolutely not prepared for that particular conversation. As to the prisoners of the 12th of July, there is a state of fact there, and we did not check this out, in view of the documents that we have been given, and they are not in line with what Mr. Butler is going to testify to. So I would put that in the same basket as the Professor Radinovic testimony. As to the other two conversations, I think that we could avail ourselves of the presence of Mr. Butler for that, and then later on the presence of our own expert, who would go into an explanation of this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a break. I should like to take advantage of the opportunity, if I may, Mr. Visnjic, to correct you. I heard that the calendar was imposed -- you say the calendar was imposed by the Chamber. The calendar was decided after consultation with both parties. So I want to say that, and that is why I spoke of calendar. The calendar was decided by the Chamber, but having held consultations by all parties concerned, which means that it was aligned with all our requirements. I think that the most judicious thing to do now would be to take a pause, and I think this will give a chance to all parties to deliberate. So if you cannot reach an agreement, the Chamber will confer, but let us take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a decision. Do you have an agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, we tried, as we always have with counsel, and we weren't able to reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, we're going to make our decision. The Chamber is hereby rendering its decision regarding the testimony of Mr. Butler. The Chamber understands that Defence has not been notified of a number of questions which the Prosecutor wishes to address now with this witness and, therefore, opposes his testifying on these new issues. However, the Chamber notes that the Defence indicated that it is ready and can accept the fact that Mr. Butler will be speaking about the issue of conversations. The Chamber therefore decide as follows: Number one, the Prosecutor shall be able to ask questions regarding conversations. The Prosecutor could not ask questions of Mr. Butler concerning the existence of prisoners on the 12th of July, 1995, or concerning the deposition of Professor Radinovic. However, to the extent Mr. Butler can make himself easily available and the Defence is, as of now, notified of the questions that the Prosecutor wanted to ask of this witness concerning the relevant issues, in view of that, the Chamber decides that if and only if a certain period of time is found in the week of the 2nd to the 6th of April envisaged for the rejoinder for the Defence and the witnesses of the Chamber, so if there is available time during that week, Mr. Butler may be called to appear once again as a witness and testify about the said issues. You have heard the decision of the Chamber. Mr. McCloskey, are we ready to hear the witness, to have the witness brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and it will be very brief. The one conversation regarding -- that I intended to ask him questions about was the Bogicevic-Zivanovic conversation. The others I hadn't intended, and I hadn't intended to ask him about tactical or operational groups. We had decided that was never relevant, and I don't have those documents. So all I need to ask him about now would be just very briefly on this intercept, and it was just to clarify a simple point in this one intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, let us hear your examination-in-chief, please. Let us have the witness brought in. Otherwise, we will spend the whole day debating about what are we going to say or hear from the witness. Let us have the witness brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get Exhibit 862/A prepared. And 86 -- well, just 862/A. I'm sorry. That's the wrong exhibit. That's the old one. 884/A. We need also the US representative here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we ready now to proceed? Mr. Butler, good morning. We already know each other. This testimony will be considered as a continuation of your previous testimony. Let me remind you of what it means. It is a testimony under an oath, and I hope you are aware of it. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Butler, you will first be answering questions that will be put to you by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, could you review Exhibit 884/A, an intercept I believe you are familiar with from the last few days.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you could, what is your analysis regarding this intercept? How does it fit into your analysis, if it does? And perhaps you could clarify -- just before you get into your analysis, can you tell, in this conversation, where General Zivanovic is speaking from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Looking at this intercept within the context of my previous analysis of the intercept events on 15 July 1995, I believe this particular intercept supports the contention that I made that by the early morning hours of 15 July 1995, General Zivanovic is aware that he is no longer commanding the Drina Corps. In that context, looking at the other intercepts and other information that we have, I do not believe that General Zivanovic is in Belgrade, as he says he is in the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what in particular is it that leads you to believe that General Zivanovic knows he's not in command any more?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The phrase - and guess put it on the ELMO would be the first way - where he notes that: "At this point I have liberated Srebrenica and now I've got a new duty."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you remind the Court and the -- this is a 1051, 15 July intercept. Also heard, the intercepts of 15 July between Zivanovic and Colonel Beara immediately prior to the conversation between Beara and Krstic. Where does this fit in in time with those conversations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In time sequence, I believe this fits in approximately one hour later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That's all the questions I have on that particular intercept subject. Mr. Butler, you became familiar with the so-called August 2nd "Kill them all" conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Approximately when did you first become familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I believe I became aware of its existence, in the audio form that the Office of the Prosecutor had it, would probably be certainly by the spring of 1999. It may have been back earlier that I got an inkling of it, but I couldn't be exactly sure, but certainly no later than the spring of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you take some time to review that and analyse that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Not at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you at some later time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Certainly as I was going into the broad aspect of analysing that, as well as all of the intercepts, and that process would have been the late period of 1999, I believe it would have been. I mean, essentially I got -- the first series of intercepts were coming out of the production and translation phase by May/June 1999 and then through the end of the year. At that point, I reviewed that, as well as hundreds of other intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this particular intercept was a subject of some debate between yourself, and discussion between yourself, other members of the staff, including the legal staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Oh, absolutely, yes. I mean, it was recognised certainly by me, certainly by the investigative team, and certainly by the legal staff, as an extremely powerful piece of information that, if it could be authenticated, would make an effective exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what's your analysis of this -- of the meaning and significance of this particular intercept, in your final analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Within -- the problem in doing a final analysis on that individual exhibit is that when you look at it in context with all of the other exhibits and when you look at it in context with all of the other material, particularly that that was included in my narrative and things of that nature, it's not the type of a piece of information that readily lends itself to my individual analysis in being able to put context to either events on the ground, or other documents, or anything else. In effect, it's a piece of information whose value I, as a military analyst, cannot ascertain along analytical methods. I have my opinion as to what it is, and at the end of the day that's my personal opinion of what it is but it is not an opinion that I could support based on the other information that's available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is your personal opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that what you're listening to in that audio intercept is an example of General Krstic giving an illegal order at face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view, was it open to any other interpretation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You said "illegal" or -- because the transcript says -- no. It's corrected now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes. Unlawful order, sir. Illegal. Is it open to another interpretation? Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You were generally not asked for your opinion regarding mental states or legal elements, were you, Mr. Butler?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I was not asked, and had I been asked, I would have shied away from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Is there another possible military interpretation of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Given the information that is available, particularly the limited information that we have pertaining to the 1st and 2nd August combat reports of the Zvornik Brigade, it's quite conceivable that the action that they're talking about -- one, the actual event that they're talking about is some form of a raid or some form of an infiltration by Bosnian Muslim 2nd Corps forces into the front lines of the Zvornik Brigade, in which case they were engaged and withdrew after hitting the minefield. As to the actual wording of General Krstic himself, there is certainly an interpretation, and one that I cannot refute, that what he was doing was euphemistically encouraging Obrenovic on, and that neither General Krstic intended it as an unlawful order or that Major Obrenovic did not take it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your mind, is it clear in that intercept that Obrenovic actually has prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Based on that intercept alone, as well as the 1st and 2nd August information that I have, I can't say that he has prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If Obrenovic doesn't have prisoners, what does the statement "Kill them all" three times mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In that regard, I would have to default back to: The context of what we're talking about is, you know, a military commander encouraging a subordinate to press his defence vigorously and to ensure that none of the members of the infiltration team, if in fact that's what it is, will be able to penetrate the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Who, in your view, is in the best position to tell us what that intercept means?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That one would be General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this intercept mentioned in your report, your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: For the most part because, as I look at it, and understanding it was a powerful exhibit, at the end of the day, when I was making my final selection of those intercepts that I wanted to use in the narrative, because I could directly relate them to the events, to the crime scene, to General Krstic, that one tended to fall outside. I mean at the end of the day, I understand that -- my firm belief is that it is, in fact, authentic. So that wasn't a motivating factor of why I included it and why I did not. But at face value and given the multiple interpretations, for me, first of all, I cannot tie it to a criminal act associated with Srebrenica. It certainly falls outside with respect -- related to Zepa. As I've indicated, I can't forward to the Court an opinion what I think it is, being either an unlawful order or anything else. I had no other information to put around it. And given the fact that at the end of the day the ultimate value of what that conversation meant or didn't mean couldn't be put into context by me as a military analyst, could only be put into context by the defendant, for me it was a logical determination that that didn't need to go into my report. At another level, I considered that if I had forwarded it, it would be looked at as a gratuitous slap against the defendant, where I would be offering up an opinion that not only could I not substantiate, but to invite the Court to look at it in the most sinister light, and I didn't believe that that was fair. If I had been able to do that, if I had been able to make those connections - I'm not -- I'm not that charitable a person - I would have it included it in my report and I would have offered it to the Court in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You're aware of the Prosecution's decision strategically to save this intercept and use it during the cross-examination with General Krstic, are you not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was your report written before that strategic decision was made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The report was being authored in various draft forms through that decision-making process. I'm not sure that there's a point in time either before or after that decision was made. I understand that the Prosecution, particularly the trial lawyers, were very interested and wanted to use that as a piece of evidence on cross-examination. I mean, they looked at it as that was its most powerful benefit. And at the end of the day, I always felt that I reserved the right myself, as the military analyst for the team, that if I needed that information in my narrative, that I was going to put it there. And at the end of the day, I don't know exactly at a point in time that occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever have this conversation in any of your drafts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: This intercept was never in any version of my drafts of the narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Allow me to take this opportunity to bid good morning to the representative of the American government, for the record, please. Let me give the floor to the Defence for the cross-examination now. Mr. Visnjic, it seems to me, is going to be cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, in response to a question put to you by Mr. McCloskey, you stated that the conversation conducted between General Krstic and Jevdjevic and Obrenovic was not included in your report. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The August conversation was not included in my report, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: The interview which General Krstic gave to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 18th and the 19th of February, is that report also -- that interview also included in your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir, I do not believe I included any material from General Krstic's interview in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Did you use that material? I don't mean whether you quoted, but did you refer yourself to the material connected with the interview of General Krstic while composing your report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I was intimately familiar with the material. I had watched the interview as it was being conducted, on closed-circuit television, and I frequently referred to the transcripts of the interview, as I've done with many other interviews and all other information, but I did not feel it's my place to include or try to manoeuvre portions of General Krstic's interview and then try to interpret what he said for the Court. I mean, at the end of the day, I didn't do that with any of the human witnesses at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were familiar with the portion of the statement of General Krstic concerning the issue of war prisoners and his attitude to that issue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I believe I am broadly, but it's awhile back and there's a lot back there, but, generally, I'm familiar with it. If you have the specific transcripts, I'm sure I can go right to it and not guess, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, wasn't it natural that somewhere in paragraph [sic] 10 of your -- I know you remember your report very well, but somewhere in paragraph 10, that is to say, between paragraphs 10 and 11 and 1021 or going on to the end of that particular paragraph, which includes in quite a lot of detail the status of the prisoners of war, was it not natural that in that portion you include the intercepted conversation by way of information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I assume you're talking about chapter 10, not paragraph 10, as is coming up on the transcript, where I talk about specifically the known status of prisoners of war in the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigade. I believe that all of the information based on that is based on documentary records, and it discusses the status of known prisoners captured through 31 July 1995. Trying to take that particular intercept, which again at face value in no way, shape, or form refers to prisoners, it doesn't fit for me. Unless I'm confused. Are you asking whether or not I should have taken General Krstic -- accounts of his interview into that for chapter 10? If that's the question, then the answer would be I wouldn't have done that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Does this also relate to paragraph 937, in which you also mention that General Krstic coordinated and received information with respect to issues connected to prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic, I apologise for interrupting. I want to ask Mr. Butler whether you would like to have your report in front of you in order to be able to answer the questions being put to you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I would appreciate that, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you indicate to us the exhibit number, please, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There's no problem. We just want to know the exhibit number so that we can show the document to Mr. Butler. Madam Registrar, can you tell us the exhibit number, please? I think it was 400 and -- Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Keith has it, and we can provide that to Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And can you tell us the exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: 403, Your Honour. What paragraph again, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In the context of paragraph 937, I would not have mentioned it in so much as the fact that the period that we're discussing is the period during which the executions are known to be occurring, within the window of 13 to 17 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Butler, you have certainly listened through many or reviewed many intercepts from both sides. In the sense of combat activity and combat action, fighting and encouragement to the soldiers, the subordinates, co-fighters, fellow fighters, these words, "Kill them all," is that mentioned fairly often? Are they frequently mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Within the confines of the intercepts on all sides, again in the heat of combat, those types of bombastic statements are mentioned very frequently. It is not a unique -- in the sense of things of that nature, you know, "Kill them all," in the sense of, "Make sure that the enemy's totally destroyed," things of that nature are typical military remarks, again not only in the context of the intercepts but in my own background as a military officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, I should like to go back to the first conversation. It is Prosecution Exhibit 884.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It's on the ELMO, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I think the Defence agrees with your conclusion that General Zivanovic did not -- was not speaking from Belgrade, that is to say that at that point in time he was not located in Belgrade. Can you be more specific and tell us where, in your opinion, General Zivanovic was when he had this conversation?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Based on this intercept alone, I cannot do that. However, based on the context of the other material that is available and the other intercepts, and given the fact that this is an hour after an intercept which I place General Zivanovic in Vlasenica, given the same series of intercepts, the same network on which the intercept was taken off of, and everything else, I believe I can state confidently that at 10.51 on 15 July, General Zivanovic is in the headquarters of the Drina Corps in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it possible, Mr. Butler, that General Zivanovic, up until that time, had received the order from President Karadzic on relieving him of his duties, or whether he became informed or learnt of this order in any other way? You can give us a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Let me just read the question again. It was a long question. I'd just like to read it on the monitor, if you don't mind. The information that I have leads me to believe that he learned earlier than 15 July that he was being relieved of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My question was whether it was possible -- whether it is possible that General Zivanovic, up until the 15th of July, that is to say, the time when this conversation took place, whether he was in a position to learn of the order by President Karadzic. So I'm talking about that particular document, not the other information, actually.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It is possible in that respect, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it also possible that part of the conversation which General Zivanovic has with Bogicevic, and which I'll now paraphrase, relates to something of the kind, "I have now been given a new assignment," is it possible that that part of the conversation is linked to the directive, the decree by President Karadzic? Order, the order. Let me say order, the order of President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: If you look at those two individual exhibits, yes, you can make a linkage possibility, yes, sir

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Butler. Mr. President, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any additional questions? If so, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Very well. Thank you very much. Judge Fouad Riad has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Butler, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just would like to have more clarification of your statements. First when you spoke about General Zivanovic being aware that he was relieved from command, I think you -- you concluded from -- you said, "I conclude from information --" You said exactly, "The information that I have leads me to believe that he knew that he was relieved before the 15th of July." All that we heard from you is that he said, "I have liberated Srebrenica and have other duties." Now, do you think the fact that he said they have other duties means that he left the Drina Corps, he can have still other duties in the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: When I made that comment, what I was envisioning was the other information, being the series of previous intercepts, as well as other documents that go back not only from 15 July, but prior to that, 14 and 13, which would lend to General Zivanovic having an understanding that he was no longer the Commander of the Drina Corps and that at a point in time the orders would follow. In date sequence, the order appointing General Krstic is dated the 14th, I believe. It's been a while with the information, but I believe it's the 14th, effective on the 15th. So clearly he also would have found out about that perhaps a little bit earlier than actually receiving the zone. The order, again if I recall correctly, on 15 July relieving General Zivanovic makes it clear that he's placed his technical status on disposal to the Main Staff, which means that at a point in time to be determined, that he would be expected to report to the Main Staff for whatever further duties the Main Staff had in mind for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And now with regard to the intercept, "Kill them all," the "Kill them all" conversation, first, your firm belief that it was authentic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What did you build this belief on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: As I testified in my direct testimony close to a year ago, when I looked at not only that intercept, but when I looked at all of the intercept information, I set up mentally in my own mind a series of checklists and parameters which the material would have to go through before I would be satisfied on that. As I noted before the Court prior, I do have considerable experience dealing with military material, including communications intercepts, which is what these are. I mean, at the end of the day, these are voice communications intercepts. I have dealt with these in the past, and I am very cognisant of the types of procedures that are used within community -- my military community that we use to validate these. Much of the validation occurs, as the Prosecution has put on through its direct case and further on in its rebuttal case, the knowledge and the technical aptitude of the actual collectors, the equipment, their understanding of the target environment, and that, for me, is the first critical piece. Again, do the collectors, do the technical collectors themselves understand what they're collecting, do they have the equipment that's capable of doing that, do they understand what the target environment is? In a way, going back after the fact makes it, in my mind, makes it easier to do this. Normally, in my line of work I don't have all of the information while I'm trying to make these judgements, so in a way, being able to look back at history is a bit of a luxury for me that I don't normally have. So I was able to, in my own mind, put together a series of checklists which would allow me to check these off. Again at the same time, and as I noted in my direct testimony, I was extremely leery of these intercepts when they first came in. We don't have, or certainly didn't have in early 1997 when we first got those, a full and complete, open relationship with the Bosnian government on the passing of information. And very candidly, my default position was that I couldn't trust this material as far as I could throw it, and that it would have to undergo an extremely rigorous check on various forms of authentication before I, as an analyst, was willing to buy into the fact that what I was getting in the series of intercepts was in fact valid intercepts and not somebody's product designed to deceive me. And having again worked with intelligence information, and knowing the general rules and models which one uses to look for deception, again I set up a series of mental checklists which I used to try and determine whether or not the information that I was receiving was in fact being fed to me. It is within a military -- the military analytical way of how we do business, information is extremely hard to come by and it's looked at very jaundicedly. If you're getting a piece of valuable information from the enemy, your first thought is you're getting it because he wants you to get it, and what does that mean? So again, I looked at the material from an extremely critical eye, and as the process wore on, I became very convinced that the Bosnian Muslims did understand the target environment they were collecting on, that they did understand what they were getting. And the percentage of the take, as it were, what they were intercepting, was in fact a fair and accurate representation of the material that they felt was militarily relevant to them, not necessarily the type of information I would want as a military analyst investigating the relationship between the military and a war crime. The information was tailored to them; it was not tailored to me. So having gone through that procedure, again that was the first validation, and at the end of the day I believe the intelligence collectors of the 2 Corps understood the target environment, they know the target environment they were going after, and that the information in the notebooks and in the printouts that I used in my narrative and I talked about in my examination, and that further that the Prosecution used in order to validate other information or other intercepts in order to set the stage for that, was valid. Now, that's the first component of the validation process. On the audiotapes themselves, I also availed myself to listen to the audiotapes, and while I do not understand the language, I can say that, you know, I have actually sat at positions, I have listened to multi-channel communications being intercepted, and more importantly, the equipment of multi-channel communications that the Serbs were using, the VRS was using, wasn't unlike early generation communications equipment that the US army used when I joined in the early '80s. The background noise, as I was listening to it, was consistent with what I understood was the background noise of military multi-communications. Now, again, at the end of the day, that can be manufactured, so I don't take that as a whole lot of value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have to draw your attention to the fact that I think the witness had stepped outside his own qualifications in commenting on these intercepts, as far as I am aware. And from his background, I did not note that he was an expert in communication devices. Perhaps I'm wrong, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We take note of that, Mr. Visnjic. Thank you. Judge Fouad Riad, please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I was interested to hear from you that -- you said that the information was tailored to them, was tailored to the Muslims, to --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Why was it tailored to them? To frighten them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It was tailored to them -- not a question of the information was tailored to them. The collection process and the material garnered from the collection process was tailored for the intelligence requirements of the Bosnian army. They were collecting it for their own purposes, their own information. Again, I use that as a tool to review or look at deception operations. If the information is coming in -- it's coming in in a form of exactly what I want, exactly what I'm looking for, or tailored to my goals, that's an indicator to me of deception. But what I found, in fact, that the information that was being collected by the collection sites, being processed through and ultimately coming into the hands of the Office of the Prosecutor, was geared for their benefit, not ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, nevertheless, you said that you cannot -- you were not able to put it into context, and this is why you excluded it from your report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I cannot put this into the context of the crimes, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In fact, you added that it was unrelated to Srebrenica. You said exactly, I think, "It cannot be tied to Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
