utterances.text: The date of 2 August lays it at the back of Zepa, and again, the information in the intercept and the information that I have separate around that does not directly tie it to the criminal acts related to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Or to anything you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Or to anything I'm aware of, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You describe it as an illegal order given by Krstic.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: That is my personal opinion of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it -- in the context of the conversation, did it sound like -- did it have the appearance of an order or what you mentioned as a bombastic statement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Given the fact that the best that I can do is read it from the transcripts and because I do not understand the language - I'm not in the position to do that - again, I have to hold open both possibilities, and my analytical conclusion at the end of the day is that I can't conclude either one. My personal opinion is one thing, but, again, I don't invite the court to take weight of my personal opinion on that. The analytical conclusion is that I can't tell what that is, whether it's an illegal order or whether it's not. You know, the question was asked: "What's my personal opinion?" That is my personal opinion, but I don't invite the Court to take any weight on that. I'm not qualified to give personal opinions of General Krstic to this Chamber, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When you say it is an illegal order, the order must have a destination, must have somebody -- given someone?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's an order. If it's just a declaration, like saying like, "Let them all go to hell," for instance, it will be giving an order that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I think given the text of the order, it could be interpreted as directive in nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: As directive.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It can be determined as directive in nature. It's not that ambiguous, I do not believe, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Madam Judge Wald has the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: With regard to the first conversation between General Zivanovic and Bogicevic, why would Zivanovic want to say he was in Belgrade? I mean, what did it add to the conversation? What would be the -- is it some kind of disinformation or what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Do you have any --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: If I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: -- any supposition?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: If I have to take a supposition, I would just say he was making a facetious remark that, "I'm in Belgrade now. I don't have a mailing address at the Drina Corps any more." Again, that is a supposition based on an opinion and what other information I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You told us that when you first began to deal with intercepts, your words were you were extremely leery and then you gave us a developed rationale of how you gained more confidence as they went along. But looking at all of the intercepts, and I remember from your report the many, many, many intercepts, were there any that you ever rejected because you didn't think that they were authentic or reliable? Not because you didn't think they were material to your specific points in your report but that you just didn't feel ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: In the issue of reliability and again -- not reliability of the process or not even the reliability of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, for your own consideration.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: There were -- there were, and there remain many intercepts which I do not include that because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: They just didn't fit in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: -- I'm not able -- it's not a question of fitting in analytically, it's a question of I can't conclusively date them or I can't get them conclusively dated to my satisfaction or that the subscribers X and Y don't -- the conversation does not tie into any of the known crime scenes, criminal events, or any of the other contexts. There is other material out there that, frankly, at the end of the day, I still don't know what it means and I don't know where it fits in. And in the cases where I can make linkage, I have, but at the end of the day, the material that's not included, most of it is not included on the basis of I'm unable to reliably date it or reliably make a judgement that it has anything of any relevance either for the Defence, or for the Prosecution, for that matter, to the case in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: When you say you're not able to reliably date it, we've had extensive testimony, and I know you weren't necessarily present, but over the last couple of days, but you certainly have seen those notebooks and the dates that -- at least theoretically place conversations between certain dates, et cetera, so what's the kind of problem you would have with dating?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: To be honest, and using Exhibit 884 as an excellent example of that, going back and looking at that, the first indication that we had this intercept, I believe, is as we've gone through the process was it came in the form of a printout that was received by the Office of the Prosecutor in, I believe, May of 1999 or 2000 or just before I testified. So it would be 2000. I'm a little fuzzy on dates, I'm sorry about that. It came in the form of a printout, and going back and looking at the printout, it was clear that the date range from this was between the period of 14 to 16 July, and based on the printout alone, there was no way to conclude what date it was. And though it generally supports what I want to say in my narrative or whatever, I can't conclusively put a date on it; therefore, it's still a piece of information awaiting analysis. Now, my understanding is that sometime in December 2000, the notebook that was associated with this conversation, that originated this conversation, came in, and when you look at the notebook, it becomes quite clear I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I would wager to say there are still many bits of information that fall into that same category.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You read, I'm sure, for your report many intercepts in which General Krstic was a participant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Did you, when you read the so-called "Kill them all" one, did anything strike you as different about the portrayal or even the speech patterns, if you can get anything because there's so many little dots every place, different in that from many of the other reports in which he, at least to me, appears much more laconic or ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: It's hard for me to do that because at the end of the day, like you all, all I'm doing is reading transcripts. I don't have the opportunity to hear the conversations and understand them in their native language, so I don't know that I'm really qualified to give you an answer on that. Within the context --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I would be very uncomfortable doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question, and answer only again if you're comfortable because I don't want to go outside any bounds. But you did say in your -- that when you first came across this or when you first analysed it -- you said you didn't analyse it until late 1999, I think. Now, I understand fully your explanation of why it just didn't fall into place for your task of recording, from a military point of view, all the events which went on, but you did say yourself that you thought it would be powerful, and you knew there was a debate in the legal staff. I don't want to know anything about the backgrounds or people involved in that, but I guess my basic question, since you brought it up, was whether or not you participated in that debate with the legal staff or you're just saying you knew there was a debate in the legal staff?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I was party to those debates. I was a -- I was a major, significant party. I was fully integrated into the team and in the debates in the process, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: So was the debate -- again, I don't want to know what the -- but did the debate concern whether to use that intercept in the case in-chief?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The -- one aspect of the debate pertained to the fact that to use it in the case in-chief, if I felt that I needed it, meant that at the end of the day, the Defence would have a very long opportunity to come up with a well-rehearsed answer to what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Well, I shouldn't ask you that. You're not a lawyer, but I was going to say, isn't that what the trial process is about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Understanding that, but again from my perspective, when I look at the information -- I'm not naive as to the mechanics involved, I mean, and I guess where -- fundamentally, to frame the argument, where that information falls is as a piece of military analysis, does that piece of information assist me in allowing the Court to understand General Krstic's role as the Commander related to the crimes and everything else? Now, having said that, I also understand that as a piece of information, it can be used as an indicator of the mental state of the accused, and I'm not qualified to pass on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: I'm not asking you. Just a last question. You said you analysed in late 1999. Did this, quote, debate take place around that time, or prior to trial, I guess is what I'm saying, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: The debate took place -- not only prior to but continuing during the case, the case in-chief. The final decision ultimately on where to use it wasn't made until my narrative hit the final form, and from my point of view, I determined that I didn't need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Madam Judge Wald. Mr. Butler, I, too, have a few questions for you. As regards the Exhibit number 884, that is the conversation between Zivanovic and Bogicevic, you stated that you didn't believe that General Zivanovic was in Belgrade. My question in relation to that is: Why did you say that you believed that --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- or didn't believe that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: I would again have to put it in context of the 9.00 or I believe it's 9.51 conversations that General Zivanovic is recorded having with Colonel Beara at a textual level. Again looking at the broader aspect of the intercepts, essentially we're talking about an intercept coming off of essentially the same communications network. If Bogicevic were in Belgrade and Zivanovic were in Belgrade, it's difficult to understand how that phone call would be routed through the Drina Corps switch in the Republika Srpska. So again putting all of the technical factors as well as the other informational factors, then that leads me to conclude that he's not in Belgrade, that he's, in fact, in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that you have already to a certain extent answered my next question in response to a question put to you by Madam Judge Wald. What would have been the interest of saying he was in Belgrade if he wasn't actually there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: Again, I don't know the answer to that, sir. The best I could say is it was a facetious comment, but again, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Thank you. Another question, Mr. Butler. When the Prosecutor asked you to analyse all these intercepts, did he give you a time framework, that is, a date from which you were supposed to make your analysis until a date when you were supposed to finish your analysis? Was there a time framework, a time frame for your work, for your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: No, sir, none from the Prosecutor. Any deadlines were internally driven by myself. I mean with that intercept, the driving force between when I -- when I looked at it and why was not relative to that intercept but it was relative to the fact that as an analytical practice, I was waiting for the entire series from July of 1995. I did not want to fall into an analytical trap of looking at pieces of intercepts in isolation, and I remember conversations in May where I was discussing the issue with Ms. Frease, telling her that, "I can't look at the intercepts until I get the entire month of July. What's taking you so long?" So in that respect, the decision to do that, when it was analysed and in what context, was entirely my own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question, for you,

utterances.speaker: MR. BUTLER
utterances.text: As regards the "Kill them all" intercept, General Krstic said that it was a rigged, that it was a montage, a 100 per cent montage. That was the word he used. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER
utterances.text: At the end of the day and as I've discussed at some length in response to Judge Riad's question, and especially when General Krstic made that statement, again as an analyst, what I did is internally to what end, set up a series of theoretical scenarios: Assuming that this is a montage, one, how do I prove that and to what end? Who is the target audience and why? Then I looked at all of the factors on how the tapes came into the OTP possession, and at the end of day there are two tapes. And as the Prosecution has laid out, I'm not sure. It came in fits and starts through a series of witnesses, but at the end of the day, when you look at the series of circumstances, how the first tape came into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor, which was recorded off of one network, and how the second tape several years later came in, and particularly in the circumstances of the second tape, you know, being lost in an archive, essentially being found by an investigation team that's investigating Muslim war crimes and the fact that it had been mislabelled and effectively lost to indexers, at the end of the day, the series of circumstances of events is almost fantastic. It comes to -- for as much difficulty and trouble as it was trying to get all these things and put all these things together, if it was going to be a montage, particularly the second tape, if you were going to go all the time and all the effort and all of the money and all of whatever it takes to do that, and again I could lay awake at nights and think of ways to do this, at the end of the day, I wouldn't mislabel the tape and lose it in an archive and hope that out of the blue somebody finds it, particularly a team that's not even investigating Serbian war crimes, one that's investigating Muslim war crimes. So again, at the end of the day, with deception, you never have an absolute indicator. There are none. At the end of the day, as an analyst what you're doing, what I do as an analyst, is it's a balance of probabilities. And in this case, given the balance of probabilities, and given everything I know about it, I'm fairly certain this is not a montage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Butler. We have no further questions for you. You have answered a number of questions by both parties and the Judges. Thank you very much for having spared some time to be with us and assist us in our work. Thank you very much once again. We wish you a lot of success in your future work. Let me also thank Mr. Alan Weiner. I hope that the name will now be entered in the record, because the first time I mentioned it, it was not reflected in the record. Thank you also for having been with us today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just like to add it's been a privilege to be at the service of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: For us too. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm told that Exhibit 884 is -- well, it's in a notebook. 884 is the conversation. So I think we would offer that into evidence to make sure that it's part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is awaiting a decision by the Chamber, like some other exhibits. What is the position of the Defence as regards this exhibit? Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no objections to this exhibit being made part of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections by the Defence, the Exhibit number 884 -- was that the exhibit that you were referring to? No. Yes. Very well, then. Therefore, the exhibit shall be admitted into evidence. Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have no additional evidence until later on on the video-conference. No more witnesses until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I think that you indicated that Mr. Ruez would also be one of your witnesses. I thought I saw it on your list, that I saw his name on the list, that is that he was supposed to talk about the chain of something -- chain of custody. Am I imagining?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He's listed with one sentence: "Mr. Ruez will testify about any necessary chain of custody issues." We believe we've covered these issues, and we will be withdrawing Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. We will wait until 4.00, then. But I thought that it would be a convenient time to ask the Defence: You have the decision of the Chamber regarding the testimony of Mr. Butler. Do you think that sometime during the day you will have an opportunity or you might be prepared to ask additional questions of Mr. Butler, or shall we leave it really for the last -- the final week of the proceedings? Do you understand what I want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it would be very difficult for us to change our position within the past half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Very well, then. I just wanted to know that in order not to waste any time. But of course you're quite right. We will then wait until 4.00 to continue, and I believe that we will continue in courtroom number 1. Mr. Visnjic, is there anything that you wish to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only wanted to ask you if it's possible to see whether the General can be escorted to the Detention Unit now and then taken back again so that he could have some rest there, because here at the Tribunal there are no possibilities for him to have a proper rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will check with the security team and give it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is still a little question that needs to be addressed. As you know, we have two motions to reopen the case, one that was submitted by the Prosecution and the other by the Defence. Maybe we can use this time to discuss them. I could perhaps invite the parties to talk amongst themselves about a possible admission of radio intercepts. If you are able to reach an agreement, please let us know, let us notify the Chamber about it; and if you do not, the Chamber will make its ruling. But there is still this issue of reopening the case. Maybe we can give you each 20 minutes to argue the motion, and then the Judges will ask questions if they have any. I think we can now have a lunch break and then come back to the courtroom. It is true that it is possible for General Krstic to be taken back to the Detention Unit, but maybe he's willing to waive his right to be present here. Mr. Harmon, can I hear your comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was hoping to use the time after lunch to prepare for the testimony [redacted]. I'm prepared to argue the motion that we have filed with the Trial Chamber right now on the issue of reopening the case to admit forensic evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any objections as regards the proposal of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We are now going to have our break. What about the presence of General Krstic, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that General Krstic would like to remain and hear the arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We're now going to have a 50-minute break and we will come back after that, and we will try to limit the time to 20 minutes for each party to argue the motion. A 50-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon once again. The question will be the reopening of the case of either parties. As you know, there is a motion by the Prosecutor and a motion by the Defence. Prosecutor. The motion of the Prosecutor has to do with four reports connected to exhumations. The Defence objected to their admission. The Prosecutor underlines that those reports are the logical follow-on to reports earlier submitted to the Chamber and to the admission of which the Defence did not object. I should like the parties to tell us whether they have discussed the matter and whether an agreement could be reached. And the other issue that we have to discuss is whether the Defence could submit a report in writing from now until the end of the rebuttal case. So I think those are the issues that we have to address. As the first motion we're talking about, the Prosecution motion, I give the floor to Mr. McCloskey first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have been unable to reach any kind of an agreement, and Ms. Karagiannakis is here and will argue the Prosecution's motion. Mr. Harmon is busy preparing the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Karagiannakis, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to reiterate, Mr. Harmon was prepared to argue this motion before the break, but because of his obligations with the witnesses, he won't be able to do so. Your Honour, this application is as you've described it. There is no dispute about what the applicable law is. It's the Delalic test, and there are two legs to that test, and what I propose to do is briefly outline why the Prosecutor says we comply with both of the legs of the testing in Delalic and reply to some of the things the Defence has stated in their reply motion. To begin with --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Sorry. So the first leg of the test is: Is this fresh in the sense that it could not have been identified and presented in the case in-chief of the Prosecutor with the exercise of reasonable diligence? The Prosecutor submits that he did indeed -- she did indeed exercise reasonable diligence. The Prosecutor has been diligently conducting exhumations in Bosnia and Herzegovina in relation to the Srebrenica case since 1996. The complete results, as they did stand in July 2000, were presented to the Trial Chamber. These four expert reports and the summary report come from reports produced after the close of the summary exhumations last year. The Defence has stated that we have not explained the reason for the delay between the close of the case and the filing of the exhumation evidence. To the contrary, Your Honour. This was explained in the motion and illustrated by Annex A. And if you have the motion in front of you, I'd ask you to look at Annex A. What Annex A shows is the time that we actually received the completed reports, and this shows that the reports were not completed until February and March of this year, and what it also shows is that within a matter of days, these reports were immediately turned over to the Defence. Then I think usually within a matter of two weeks, the B/C/S version of the report was finalised and then again immediately provided to the Defence, so that as soon as we did receive those reports, we forwarded them. The reason for the delay was because the experts needed time to consider their findings, and this is set out in our motion. As you know, it's not possible to produce an expert -- a considered expert report immediately after work is finished. Autopsies need to be concluded and the experts need to consider their results. So for those reasons, Your Honour, I submit that we have been diligent in providing -- in getting the evidence, the exhumation evidence, and then immediately providing it over to the Defence. There is another point that is mentioned in the reply of the Defence, and that is that there's an implication that we, by our own decision regarding the allocation of resources, didn't conduct these exhumations properly. I think what the defendant said is the speed of the exhumation is directly related to the resources that the Prosecutor has chosen to allocate to that task. That's in paragraph 6 of their reply. Your Honour, as you have become aware, this Srebrenica case involves numerous execution sites and many, many graves, and our investigation is not the only investigation. However, despite the limited resources that the Office of the Prosecutor has had, has diligently conducted exhumations since 1996 in Bosnia, so that this is not a fair criticism and doesn't -- and this argument doesn't have merit. Your Honours, I'm now going to turn to the issue of the probative value, which is the second leg of the Delalic test. The defendant -- the Prosecutor says that this evidence has probative value and has set out exactly what that probative value is in paragraphs -- in paragraph 9 of its submission. Now, the Delalic test says that you must weigh the probative value of the evidence against the -- effectively the prejudicial effect or the fairness of the trial, prejudicial effect on the accused and the fairness of the trial. This evidence is probative. It goes to genocide. It shows an increased number of bodies. It shows that the people in those graves were executed because we've discovered further ligatures and blindfolds. And it also shows two important linkages, and that is the linkage between the primary grave site and execution site of Orahovac and the secondary grave sites at Hodzici, 3, 4, and 5, and also another very new and interesting piece of evidence, which is a direct --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: -- physical link from the Glogova 1 site to the Kravica warehouse, so that part of a door frame from the warehouse was found in the grave, and this is extremely probative value linking an execution site to a grave site. The Defence has said that this isn't really -- this is -- the probative value of this evidence is quite slight and cumulative. Well, it's cumulative in the sense that we've already adduced much of the same type of evidence, but it's my submission that, in particular, the linkage evidence is not cumulative. It adds yet another important linkage between execution site, and therefore executioner, to mass grave site, and in another case mass grave site to secondary grave site. So you're looking at linkages between execution, grave site, and cover-up, and those are very critical for the consideration of liability in this case. It's further submitted that it's not at all unfair to the defendant to produce this in writing if they have also an opportunity to reply in writing, because four out of the five people that are submitting the reports have been cross-examined in this Court by the Defence. The defendant and Defence counsel has never -- has not contested the fact that executions occurred. And critically, Your Honour, I take you to page 7, paragraph 7 of our submission, where we set out that Dr. Stankovic has agreed that the exhumations and autopsies were conducted with professionalism and according to scientifically-accepted methodology, which means that he's accepted the professionalism of four out of our five experts. He also says, and I quote, in his report, the ligatures -- in response to the previous exhumations evidence we've put in: "The ligatures tying the hands, wrists, or blindfolds registered in the bodies, and the injuries ascertained to the soft tissues and bones inflicted by the bullets or other mechanical tool, is a sure sign that such persons, after being captured, were shot or killed in other way." So that's an acceptance by the Defence's own expert that people lying in the exhumation -- in the graves that we have presented evidence about were executed. And I think that -- we think that that is a very critical admission that the Trial Chamber should take into account when considering to admit this further evidence, which is cumulative in some ways and does provide extra important ligature evidence in other ways. And when exercising your discretion, Your Honours, I'd ask you to exercise it in terms of Rule 90(F), which states that: "The Trial Chamber should exercise control over the mode and order of the presentation of evidence so as to make the interrogation and the presentation effective --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little slower, please, counsel. The interpreters are not able to follow at that speed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Rule 90(F) states that the Trial Chamber should exercise its discretion so as to ascertain the truth, and it is the Prosecutor's submission that this extra exhumations evidence allows the ascertainment of truth. The second part of Rule 90(F) says that the Trial Chamber should exercise its discretion to avoid the needless consumption of time. It is the Prosecutor's submission that there would not be needless consumption of time in this case if the evidence were to be allowed to come in in written form and if the Defence were permitted to then reply in written form. The Prosecutor is prepared to accept a written reply to this additional evidence, and should that reply not be possible in their -- or orally in their surrebuttal case or in written form before their surrebuttal case, we would be prepared to accept it at some later date. If that date were to exceed the filing time of the closing written arguments, which is the 20th of April, we would then enjoin the Court to exercise its discretion to allow a further -- to allow further filings in respect of this additional evidence by the Defence. In this way -- and such filing should be obviously before the final oral arguments. In this way, Your Honours, you would be permitted to allow this new evidence in without unduly extending the length of the trial and without prejudicing the right of the accused to reply to the exhumation evidence presented. Your Honour, I have one final submission to make. It was suggested in the reply of the Defence that we ought to have provided those reports pursuant to Rule 94 bis, the implication being we should have presented this in our rebuttal case, which is being conducted now. It's my submission that it is quite apparent from Annex A in terms of -- to our brief in terms of when we received the reports and when we finally received them in B/C/S that we would have not been able to comply with the time periods set out in 94 bis to present it in our case. So we did it in this manner instead, seeking to reopen in written form. Further, we had already scheduled quite a number of witnesses for our rebuttal case, Your Honours, and it would not have been possible to have added another five witnesses, four of which had already been cross-examined by the Defence and their expert conclusions largely accepted in terms of executions. So those are the reasons why, despite the exercise of our reasonable diligence, we could not present this information according to that Rule. That concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: There aren't any more in the pipeline, are there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Karagiannakis. The response from the Defence. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence will refrain from repeating its arguments in its response to the application of the Prosecution to reopen its case. We shall just try to explain to Your Honours that we understand this application as one that affects the use of the time that we have left until the close of the case. If the Prosecution needed the time from August, when some exhumations were completed, until March this year, to provide the Defence with these reports, and in doing so the Prosecution, as she does on page 68 of this LiveNote, to limited resources at the disposal of the Prosecution, then we have to underline that our resources, as compared to those of the Prosecution, are many times more limited. Our expert was given a number of reports in the Serbo-Croatian language just before the Prosecution filed its application. In my opinion, it is still difficult to assess how much time he would need to study those reports so as to be able to decide whether the Defence will file an objection pursuant to Rule 94 bis. On the other hand, the Defence has no prejudice regarding the future report of its expert regardless of his earlier statements here before this Trial Chamber, and on the other hand, the Defence also knows that he has presented numerous criticisms of the expert report of the Prosecution in his submission -- in his report of the 17th of October, 2000. I can only assume that he will have some critical remarks to make, but that is up to him, and we would like to leave it up to him as the expert to do so. Bearing in mind the need for efficient use of time under Rule 90(F)(ii), that is to avoid needless consumption of time, the question remains as how much time the Defence would need -- should the Trial Chamber grant the request of the Prosecution, how much time the Defence would need to make a considered analysis of the Prosecution's report. So I would like to summarise our position, and that is that we are opposed to the reopening of the Prosecution's case on the basis of all the grounds submitted in our response of the 20th of March, 2000. On the other hand, in response to your question, Your Honour, we are ready, should the Trial Chamber so decide, to accept the application of the Prosecution and to provide further evidence in written form as we did in the course of the Prosecution case in-chief. What I would like to point out is that the time given to us to deal with this problem is many times smaller than the Prosecution had for its preparations in view of the provisions of Rule 94 bis, on the one hand, and on the other, that the resources available to the Defence are also far more limited than those at the disposal of the Prosecution. For those reasons, the Defence appeals to Your Honours to take all these arguments into consideration when bringing your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Ms. Karagiannakis, is there something that you should like to add, but very briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Two very brief comments, Your Honour. First of all, when experts go to Bosnia to conduct exhumations, they do not leave the field until approximately October, at the end of the year. And the second comment is with respect to resources. Obviously, it takes a lot more time to conduct exhumations than to reply to the methodology and the conclusions that result from the physical evidence taken from those exhumations. However, the Prosecutor does agree that the Defence ought to have a reasonable time to review our reports. These reports have indeed been provided to them in March and in February, and it is our view that with the scheduling that I proposed earlier, a reasonable time would be allowed to them and their expert to provide such additional written reports. Perhaps just one more comment, Your Honour. We agreed to Dr. Stankovic's report being filed as a piece of evidence in this case without calling him to trial, and we replied to his criticisms, minor criticisms, of our experts' reports in writing. So it has been done before, and it's our submission that it should be done again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Karagiannakis. So we will review all that has been said, and we will make a ruling. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is one more issue that we have some hesitation about and that is when the time begins to run, that is, the 15-day time limit according to Rule 94 bis for the Defence. Actually, we have two possibilities, either that it begins to run from the moment the Trial Chamber makes its decision, should it grant the request of the Prosecution, or would that time begin to run from the moment the Prosecution filed its request? Of course, we would prefer the former solution in view of the fact that until a Trial Chamber makes a decision, we are not in a position to anticipate something that is still uncertain. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Visnjic. Ms. Karagiannakis, do you have any comments to that? No? I see a negative sign from the Prosecution bench. So we'll go on to the motion of the Defence now. Yes. Madam Judge Wald tells me that as we're going to discuss matters which could affect certain confidential information disclosed in private session, we should conduct our discussions in private session as well. So let us go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: ---Recess taken at 2.10 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: at 7.58 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 2nd day of April, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 25
